    GameChange Solar Corp. v. United States (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00174 / USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00174-0

    FAPD-AI: The Court of International Trade denied GameChange Solar Corp.'s challenge to an International Trade Administration determination that the company's off-grid solar charging module is within the scope of antidumping and countervailing duty orders on crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells from China. The court found that the charging module, which contains crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells and is described by GameChange as a module, falls within the scope language covering modules of such cells assembled into other products. The court rejected GameChange's arguments that the product qualified for a consumer good exclusion or an off-grid photovoltaic panel exclusion. USCOURTS-SEL-02

      United States v. Hebert (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-24-07030 / USCOURTS-ca10-24-07030-0

      FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit vacated Dennis Hebert's conviction for aggravated sexual abuse in Indian country. The court held the government failed to produce sufficient evidence to prove Hebert's non-Indian status beyond a reasonable doubt. Proof of non-Indian status is an essential element of the offense under 18 U.S.C. § 1152. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    • Observed at 20:48:37 Eastern time ET
      United States v. Hebert (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-24-07030 / USCOURTS-ca10-24-07030-1

      FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit held en banc that in a prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 1152 where the victim is an Indian, the defendant's Indian status constitutes an affirmative defense that the defendant must prove by a preponderance of the evidence. The court overturned its prior decision in United States v. Prentiss II, which had required the government to prove the defendant's non-Indian status as an essential element of the offense. The cases were remanded for further proceedings, including possible retrials. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 20:48:37 Eastern time ET
    Lewis, et al v. United States (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-01036 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-01036-0

    FAPD-AI: Kate Lewis sought damages for negligent misdiagnosis of breast cancer at a federally funded clinic in 2017, which allegedly delayed her treatment and worsened her prognosis. The Tenth Circuit reversed summary judgment for the United States, finding that one of the statutory exceptions to Colorado's three-year statute of repose for medical malpractice claims applied to her case. The matter was remanded for further proceedings. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 20:48:37 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Cota-Higuera (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-02083 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-02083-0

    FAPD-AI: Hector Abraham Cota-Higuera, a federal inmate serving a 15-year sentence, sought to vacate his sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255, arguing his trial counsel failed to consult with him about filing an appeal. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of the motion, finding that counsel consulted with Cota-Higuera about his appeal rights and Cota-Higuera did not provide express instructions to pursue an appeal. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    United States v. Griego (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-02085 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-02085-0

    FAPD-AI: Dennis Griego sought a certificate of appealability to challenge the denial of his motion to vacate an Armed Career Criminal Act sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255. The Tenth Circuit denied the certificate, concluding that Griego failed to demonstrate a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right and that the Supreme Court's decision in Erlinger v. United States announced a new rule that was not apparent to reasonable jurists when his conviction became final in 2018. USCOURTS-SEL-01

      United States v. Ruiz (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-24-02128 / USCOURTS-ca10-24-02128-2

      FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit en banc overturned prior precedent and held that in prosecutions under 18 U.S.C. § 1152 where the victim is Indian, the defendant's Indian status is an affirmative defense that the defendant must prove by a preponderance of evidence, rather than an element the government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt. The court vacated panel opinions in two cases and remanded for further proceedings consistent with this ruling. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:47 Eastern time ET
    Attorney General, State of Florida, Department of v. SNAP (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12814 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12814-0

    FAPD-AI: Florida's Attorney General sued Snap Inc. in state court for violating HB3 by contracting with minors under age 14. Snap removed the case to federal court claiming federal officer removal jurisdiction based on advertising services provided to federal agencies and also asserting diversity jurisdiction. The Eleventh Circuit held the district court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the removal and remanded the case to state court, finding Snap's relationships with federal agencies insufficient to establish federal officer removal status. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:47 Eastern time ET
    Kathleen Watrel v. W. Cooper, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10430 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10430-0

    FAPD-AI: Kathleen Watrel appealed the dismissal of her complaint against judges and others and her denied motion for the district judge to recuse himself. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding that the state court judges were entitled to judicial immunity because her allegations related to their official judicial actions, and that Watrel failed to meet the standards for recusal under federal law. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:46 Eastern time ET
    Computer & Communications Industry Association, et al v. Attorney General, State of Florida (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-11881 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-11881-0

    FAPD-AI: The Computer & Communications Industry Association and NetChoice challenged Florida's HB3, which restricts social media platforms using certain features—including infinite scrolling, push notifications, and auto-play—from allowing minors under 14 to create accounts and requiring parental consent for ages 14-15. The Eleventh Circuit held that the industry organizations had standing to pursue their First Amendment challenge, that Younger abstention did not apply, and that the statute as applied likely constitutes a content-neutral speech regulation satisfying intermediate scrutiny. The court rejected the facial challenge to the law. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:44 Eastern time ET
    Christopher Bonner v. Timothy Ward, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-13016 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-13016-0

    FAPD-AI: Christopher Mathis died in a segregation unit at Georgia State Prison after an attack by another inmate. His son brought a section 1983 suit under the Eighth Amendment against prison officials, claiming violations based on conditions of confinement, inadequate staffing, and failure to protect from other prisoners. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of the complaint, finding Mathis did not plausibly allege unconstitutional conditions and that no causal connection existed between prior threats and the fatal attack. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:44 Eastern time ET
    Ebony Kelley v. Allegiant Air, LLC. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-13815 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-13815-0

    FAPD-AI: Ebony Kelley, a Black employee of Allegiant Air, sued for race discrimination and retaliation under 42 U.S.C. section 1981 after being terminated for dishonesty during an investigation into a workplace incident. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Allegiant, finding Kelley failed to establish a valid similarly-situated comparator for her discrimination claim and failed to present evidence that Allegiant's stated reason for termination was pretextual. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:43 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Friell Johnson (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-21-14144 / USCOURTS-ca11-21-14144-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit vacated Friell Johnson's sentence for firearm possession as a felon because the district court incorrectly calculated his base offense level by classifying his prior attempted manslaughter conviction as a crime of violence under the sentencing guidelines. Attempted manslaughter does not qualify as an enumerated crime of violence under the guideline definition. The court rejected Johnson's facial challenge to the firearm possession statute under the Second Amendment. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:33:43 Eastern time ET
    Carlos Figueroa-Gibson v. Warden (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-10658 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-10658-0

    FAPD-AI: Carlos Figueroa-Gibson, a federal prisoner convicted of attempted child sex trafficking, filed a habeas petition challenging the First Step Act's bar on earning early-release credits for prisoners with certain convictions, claiming violations of due process and equal protection rights. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of the petition, holding that Figueroa had no constitutionally protected liberty interest in credits he was never eligible to earn and that the statute's classification system did not violate equal protection. The court found his procedural due process claim failed because the Act conditions credit eligibility on the nature of the conviction. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Public Law 119–36: To amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to prevent consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consum… (opens in a new tab)
    Enacted law · govinfo API · PLAW-119publ36

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 119-36, the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act, amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to restrict consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports in certain circumstances related to residential mortgage lending. The law prohibits furnishing such reports based on a prescreening request connected to a mortgage loan transaction unless the requesting entity either holds documented consumer authorization, has originated or services the consumer's mortgage, or is a depository institution with a current account for that consumer. The law also requires the Comptroller General to study the value of trigger leads received by text message and report findings to Congress within 12 months of enactment. PLAW-SEL-01

    Public Law 119–120: To require an annual report of taxpayer-funded projects that are over budget and behind schedule. (opens in a new tab)
    Enacted law · govinfo API · PLAW-119publ120

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 119-120, titled the "Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025" and enacted on October 7, 2026, requires the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to establish guidance for federal agencies to submit annual reports on taxpayer-funded projects that are more than 5 years behind schedule or exceed their original cost estimate by $1 billion or more. The Director must compile agency submissions into an annual report to Congress and post it on the OMB website, including project descriptions, locations, contractors, scope changes, current timelines and costs, and explanations for delays or cost increases. The guidance must be issued within one year of the law's enactment. PLAW-SEL-01

    official summary: EPA is issuing significant new use rules (SNURs) under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) for certain chemical substances that were the subject of premanufacture notices (PMNs) and are also subject to an Order issued by EPA pursuant to TSCA. The SNURs require persons to notify EPA at least 90 days before commencing the manufacture (defined by statute to include import) or processing of any of these chemical substances for an activity that is designated as a significant new use in the SNUR. The required notification initiates EPA's evaluation of the conditions of that use for that chemical substance. In addition, the manufacture or processing for the significant new use may not commence until EPA has conducted a review of the required notification; made an appropriate determination regarding that notification; and taken such actions as required by that determination. Consistent with the data use requirements set forth in 34 U.S.C. 10134, no adverse determinations are made from these records as to any identifiable individual.
